reason: The chambers need muscle to squeeze blood, matching the first goal.
expectation: The muscle will surround the chambers so they can contract.

effect: The chambers can now squeeze, but fluid moves toward both openings, so valves should direct the flow.
reaction: The two-way arrows make the need for valves clear.
reason: The valves' pictured cusps close against reverse flow, matching the goal of driving blood forward.
expectation: The valves should limit reverse flow during a squeeze.

effect: The valves direct flow during squeezing and refill; the pacemaker cells look like the remaining part needed for repeated squeezes.
reaction: The paired squeeze and refill panels clarify how the valves work.
reason: The pacemaker cells produce a spreading electrical wave, which may coordinate repeated heart contractions.
expectation: The pacemaker cells should make the heart squeeze repeatedly.

effect: The pacemaker completed the beating heart, leaving the returning blood route to build.
reaction: The distinction between starting the beat and nerves adjusting it is useful.
reason: Hemoglobin binds oxygen, so it belongs inside the red-cell envelopes before the cells join the blood.
expectation: The envelopes will become oxygen-carrying red blood cells.

effect: The red blood cells can carry oxygen and make ATP without mitochondria. They now need to join the plasma.
reaction: The contrast with the muscle cells is interesting.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component available for carrying the red blood cells through the vessels.
expectation: The red blood cells and plasma should form blood.

effect: The red blood cells and plasma formed oxygen-carrying blood; the pump and vessel route still need connecting.
reaction: The picture makes the different locations of hemoglobin and dissolved sugar clear.
reason: Capillaries can connect the outgoing arteries to the returning veins to form a route.
expectation: The vessels will form a connected route through capillary networks and back toward the heart.

effect: The capillaries connected the arteries and veins into a circuit with slots for a pump and transport medium.
reaction: The marked slots make the remaining fittings clear.
reason: The beating heart fits the circuit's pump slot.
expectation: The heart will be fitted as the pump for the vessel circuit.

effect: The beating heart is fitted as the pump; the circuit still needs its transport medium.
reaction: The heart’s connections to outgoing and returning vessels make the route clearer.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood fits the remaining transport medium slot.
expectation: The blood will fill the circuit and complete the returning route.

effect: The blood completed the circuit, showing exchange with tissue and the return route to the heart.
reaction: The exchange inset usefully connects the circulation to the cells it supplies.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding valves was most worthwhile: the squeeze and refill panels showed how they direct flow, building on the earlier picture of fluid moving toward both openings.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the heart and blood into named slots was clear but predictable; those steps added less to my understanding than building the parts.

surprise.text: I was surprised that the red blood cells make ATP from sugar despite having no mitochondria, unlike the muscle cells encountered earlier.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary; the component pictures and circuit slots gave each combination a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would choose to continue for another chapter. The red-cell contrast and tissue-exchange picture made me curious how the completed circuit will support other body systems.
